terms.definition: The way some white blood cells engulf and digest pathogens.
terms.examiner: One of three white blood cell responses, with antibodies and antitoxins.

terms.definition: A protein made by white blood cells (lymphocytes) that binds to a specific antigen on a pathogen.
terms.examiner: Antibodies are specific: each fits one antigen.

terms.definition: A substance made by white blood cells that neutralises a toxin made by bacteria.
Injecting a small quantity of dead or inactive pathogen, so white blood cells make antibodies; if the real pathogen enters later, antibodies are made quickly.
terms.examiner: Herd immunity: when most of a population is vaccinated, the pathogen cannot spread easily.

terms.definition: A medicine, such as penicillin, that kills bacteria inside the body.
terms.examiner: Antibiotics cannot kill viruses, because viruses live inside cells.

terms.definition: A drug that treats the symptoms of a disease but does not kill the pathogen.
terms.examiner: Aspirin is a painkiller from willow; digitalis comes from foxgloves.

terms.definition: A trial in which neither the patients nor the doctors know who has the drug and who has the placebo.
A substance that looks like the drug but contains no drug, used as a control in a trial.
terms.examiner: Placebos are not always given to very ill patients for ethical reasons.
